title: This WRX 22B Is the Holy Grail of Subarus

body_markdown:
In *Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade,* our titular hero is tasked with a difficult choice: He must pick out the true Holy Grail from a host of potential relics. Indy selects a humble clay cup and gets it right. However, in an even better alternative universe, he reaches past this cup, past the bejeweled goblets, and grasps instead the keys to a small, blue Subaru coupe.


Then he exits the cave sideways with a roar of a turbocharged flat-four, all four wheels scrambling for grip in the sand. Behind him, the Grail Knight intones, “You have chosen… wisely.” Then he takes a hit from a vape pen and puts on a chainmail flat-brim baseball hat.


But I digress. Here it is, the Holy Grail of all Subarus, the 1998 Impreza WRX STi 22B. For a car with a name that sounds like the brand of pencil on your grade schooler’s September supply list, it’s rare, desirable, eye-wateringly expensive, and at the very tippy-top of the list of collectible Subarus.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


If you were a curator at The Petersen putting together the museum’s greatest-hits display of Japanese manufacturers, finding an example of one of these cars would be basically job one. Choosing a representative for Nissan would require picking between Skyline generations or perhaps the 240Z. The right Toyota might be a Supra, but potentially the rarer 2000GT. But Subaru? There’s only one that rules the roost.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


But is a 22B really choosing wisely? These cars have always been expensive, and the first one to be auctioned in the U.S. fetched over $300,000 at the hammer. Porsche fanatic Jerry Seinfeld is known to be fond of a high-performance Subaru or two, but perhaps even he would be hard-pressed to explain why a hopped-up Japanese compact car can justifiably pull in air-cooled 911 money.


Even so, the 22B remains the brightest star in the constellation Pleiades. For a subset of the automotive world, it’s like a Shelby Cobra, right down to the feeling that if you see one, it almost has to be a replica. But this one’s real, number 296 of 400 made.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


## Subaru’s F40 Moment


If Subaru had played its cards wrong, it might have been Saab. Instead, it seems to have turned out to be more like Volvo, selling family-friendly fare that trades on a reputation for safety. However, back in the 1970s and 1980s, it had that same Saab-like blend of aviation history and just plain oddball quirkiness.


Something like a Subaru Leone was a surefooted choice for winter driving, but it was less fashionable than cargo shorts. As far as performance went, the cars were only quicker than the competition when the competition was stuck in a snowy ditch.


All that changed with the introduction of the Legacy in 1989, and the Impreza in 1992. When equipped with the then-new EJ-series 2.0-liter turbocharged flat-four, the Legacy proved itself both swift and capable, laying down a series of endurance speed records that, incredibly, still stand.


Getty Images


Subaru didn’t really make much of these records in advertising, but it did shine the spotlight on its rallying efforts, especially when those efforts began to result in success. In 1995, a young Scottish racer named Colin McRae handed Subaru its first WRC constructor’s title, the first win for a driver from the U.K., and the youngest to do so. McRae had raced the Legacy RS too, but his championship came behind the wheel of a turbocharged Impreza, and the WRX became a household name.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Well, sort of. The North American market didn’t get the WRX until 2002, and finding WRC media coverage wasn’t the easiest for would-be rally fans. However, you could buy U.S.-market Subarus like the 2.5RS coupe that was, at least, like having a car that’s wearing a Colin McRae fan club t-shirt.


Subaru would win the WRC constructor’s championship in 1995, 1996, and 1997. With 1998 also being the company’s 40th anniversary, Subaru decided to bake itself a turbocharged rally-car-shaped cake.


## Technically, It’s a Pike Factory Car


The 22B started as a pretty standard Impreza coupe chassis, with an engine and transmission almost identical to the Japanese-market STi Type-R. For the transmission, it meant a five-speed manual with a 50:50 torque split front to rear, plus a limited-slip differential out back and a driver-controllable center diff. Subaru slightly reinforced the gearbox over the STi with shot-peened gears, an upgraded main shaft, and a twin-plate, ceramic-metallic clutch.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The engine was the same architecture as the Japanese-market EJ20 but with a 10 percent displacement bump thanks to a 4mm (0.16”) increase in the bore. The turbo is the same ball-bearing type as the Japanese-market STi, an all-rounder with a little more top end than the one found in the later U.S.-market STi. Officially, this EJ22 makes exactly the same power as pretty much every 1990s performance car in Japan, at 276 horses. *Wink, wink.*


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


In reality, it’s probably more like 300+ hp, same as with various factory Skyline GT-Rs and such. There is of course more power to be squeezed from the engine, though that’s not really required; more on this in a bit. Curb weight was 2800 pounds, less than the current BRZ but with a full all-wheel-drive system onboard. The B part of the 22B name is said to be either for the Bilstein dampers on the car, or for Subaru’s internal code for turbocharged engines.


Meantime, what sets a 22B apart from the rest of the range, and makes it such a popular silhouette for replica builders, are those perfectly flared wheel arches. They accommodate a set of 8.5-inch-wide forged BBS wheels wearing 235/40/R17 Pirellis, finished in rally-style gold, of course. The shape was penned by Peter Stevens, who also styled the actual WRC cars. All were painted Sonic Blue Mica.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


By curious quirk, the subcontractor Subaru tapped for the manufacturing and installation of these flares was Takada Kogyo, a specialist more commonly known for working with Nissan. There’s a nice bit of echo here from Subaru’s all-wheel-drive heritage, in that the original all-wheel-drive Leones were cobbled together using the rear-wheel-drive parts from a Datsun 510 (Bluebird, in the Japanese market). This also makes the 22B a cousin to the Nissan Be-1 and Figaro, as Takada Kogyo was the real-life assembler behind the fanciful Pike Factory retro-modern cars.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


Exactly 400 were made for the Japanese market, then another two dozen that found their way to the U.K., Australia, and so forth. Three prototypes were built and given to the heroes of Subaru’s rally efforts: one for McRae, one for his unflappable Welsh co-driver Nicky Grist, and one to Prodrive’s David Lapworth, whose company set up the racing cars. Subaru of America got one from the regular production run, somewhat oddly the thirteenth car, but delivered without a numbered plate.


The entire run sold out in under two days, or perhaps even as rapidly as half an hour; there are conflicting stories. With so few out in the world, the bulk of them in Japan, the 22B developed a bit of a mystic aura. For most Subaru fans, just seeing one would be a memorable event, but that was unlikely outside of a car show when Subaru of America brought its 22B.


## Hype Versus Reality


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


In the sheet metal, this is a tiny car. It has a shorter wheelbase than a BRZ by two inches, and sits low and wide. It is also handsome and well-proportioned, something you can’t really say about most Subarus, even the fast ones.


The cabin is huge and airy, with stick-thin C-pillars and a broad view ahead. It’s all business, little in the way of extra gauges, just a central tachometer dominating the display.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The owner, Charles Wong, has had Nissan GT-Rs and Silvias, and he reckons the 22B is, out of the box, even better than the Nissans. A model like the R34 GT-R is best when tuned, but in factory form, the 22B is light and lithe.


And it’s eager. The slight bump in displacement adds low- and mid-range torque, combined with a turbocharger that adds a wallop of mid-range boost. It spools up quickly like a later U.S. 2.5-liter turbocharged engine but against less weight, with an 8000 rpm redline and a five-speed gearbox with close-ratio gearing.


It all feels a bit magical, a hand-assembled machine that was the best road car Subaru could put together at a time when it was standing atop the WRC podium. Like the *Indiana Jones* franchise, the special effects budget got better later on, but the products got more forgettable.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


The only question is whether the 22B ultimately suffers for its exclusivity, in the way something like a Porsche 911 RS 2.7 does. Putting miles on the genuine article is expensive. Would a clone built out of an Impreza 2.5RS coupe offer just as much fun in a package you could actually drive and enjoy? Of course, and you could further tune it, unlock an extra 50 or so horses, throw on more modern tires, and not worry about door dings and rock chips. It’s true of any classic.


Indiana Jones wasn’t right about everything; the 22B doesn’t belong in a museum. The physical driving experience can be replicated, but that sense of history, hand-built care, and the connection to a golden age for Japanese-brand manufacturing all add up to something properly special. After all, it’s a car good enough to be the company’s gift to Colin and Nicky.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


To his credit, Wong has actually taken his 22B to various meets, including a recent gathering of the local Subaru club. Attendees were obviously thrilled to see one, even if ownership is an unobtainable goal for most mainstream Subaru fans.


Having made its way to the West Coast of Canada via Hong Kong, this car is soon headed south to a Japan-focused collection, where it’ll take its place next to Acura NSXs and rare GT-R variants and tuned Mazda RX-7s, as well as a Ferrari or two.


[Brendan McAleer](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/bmcaleer/)


It is perhaps a more humble machine than the rest of that crowd, with its compact car roots, four-cylinder engine, and tinny construction. There are stars on its badge, but it isn’t in the same constellation as exotics from Italy or even Japan’s other heroes of speed. Even so, the 22B is a Grail among Grails.
